questions.q: Why is "uptime %" alone usually a vanity metric on an incident dashboard?
options: It can show the service as healthy by its health-check definition while real user requests are failing or timing out against a saturated dependency
Uptime percentages are impossible to calculate accurately in any monitoring tool
Uptime only applies to on-premises servers, not cloud-hosted services
It changes too frequently to be rendered on a dashboard panel
questions.explain: A process can pass its health check while downstream calls time out, so uptime by that definition can look fine while users are actually being hurt.

questions.q: What are the four golden signals from Google's SRE book?
options: CPU, memory, disk, and network
Uptime, request count, deploy frequency, and ticket volume
Latency, traffic, errors, and saturation
Cost, availability, security, and compliance
questions.explain: Latency, traffic, errors, and saturation are the four signals the SRE book recommends building most service dashboards around.

questions.q: In the checkout API example, why did average response time stay normal while a real subset of users couldn't check out?
options: The average metric was being collected from the wrong region
Averaging diluted the effect of one slow backend instance's badly affected requests across many fast ones from healthy instances
Average response time cannot be measured for APIs, only for static pages
The checkout API didn't emit any latency metrics at all
questions.explain: A minority of requests being severely slow barely moves a mean calculated across all requests; a percentile like p99 is designed to expose exactly that kind of localized problem.

questions.q: What does the RED method stand for, and what is it built for?
options: Rate, Errors, Duration — the request-centric version of the golden signals, used for APIs and web services
Resource, Energy, Density — a cloud cost-optimization framework
Retry, Escalate, Deploy — an incident-response checklist
Read, Execute, Delete — a database access pattern
questions.explain: RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) is the request-centric shorthand for the golden signals, aimed at anything that serves requests.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend breaking latency panels down per endpoint or per backend instance rather than showing one aggregated line?
options: Aggregated panels load faster in every dashboarding tool
Per-endpoint breakdowns are required by the USE method and have no other purpose
An aggregate line is exactly what hides a problem that's localized to one endpoint, instance, or region
Breakdowns are only useful for cost dashboards, not reliability dashboards
questions.explain: A localized failure (one bad instance, one slow endpoint) gets diluted into near-invisibility once it's averaged together with everything that's working fine.
